title: When lilacs bloomed
hookLine: Whitman's elegy for Lincoln: lilacs, a star, a bird singing
tomorrow: what did Whitman do in the war hospitals?

cards: A singer dies, someone you never met, and the tears come in the car anyway, to your own surprise. Whitman's country had a loss like that, on a national scale. After President Lincoln was killed, Whitman wrote an elegy.
In it, a coffin travels day and night through lanes and streets, past towns and fields, while crowds stand by. And here's the strange part: in the whole poem, Lincoln's name never appears.

teach.h: WHEN LILACS LAST IN THE DOORYARD.
teach.b: It opens: "When lilacs last in the dooryard bloom'd, And the great star early droop'd in the western sky in the night, I mourn'd, and yet shall mourn with ever-returning spring."
Instead of a speech about a president, Whitman gives grief three things to hold.

teach.h: A SPRIG ON THE PASSING COFFIN.
teach.b: A sprig of lilac, broken from a bush by an old farmhouse, laid on the coffin as it passes.

teach.h: A STAR IN THE WEST, A THRUSH.
teach.b: A great star, sinking in the west. And a hermit thrush, a shy bird singing alone in the swamp, a song he can't get out of his head.
He keeps coming back to all three, and by the end they're braided together: "Lilac and star and bird twined with the chant of my soul." That's Whitman's teaching on public grief.
It's real grief, even for someone you never knew, and it needs something small and physical to carry it: a flower, a light, a song. And he widens it.
The poem mourns the dead soldiers too, and the mothers, wives and children left behind. One loss opens onto all of them.
And notice: the lilac comes back every spring. The grief returns with it, and so does the flower.

how: Some readers of Whitman turn to this elegy in times of public mourning, reading it aloud at memorials, sometimes with a sprig of lilac or another flower laid nearby.

games.q: a coworker rolls her eyes at people crying over a well-known stranger. what would Whitman's elegy say?
o: public grief is real, and it needs something small to hold: a flower, a song.
she's right; grief only counts for people you knew in person.
crying misses the point; the right response is a long speech.
games.why: Whitman answered a nation's loss with no speech at all: a lilac, a star, a bird, and the soldiers' families mourned alongside.

practice: Bring to mind one public loss that stayed with you: a singer, a leader, strangers in the news. Say the name out loud, once.
Then give it one thing to hold, the way Whitman gave a sprig of lilac: a flower, a song, a light, and let it sit beside the name.
